A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Russian-language mental-disorder detection study despite the changed title. Their complete main texts, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification experiments on five datasets, pooled-dataset evaluations, and transfer from clinically diagnosed essays to social-media data.

after.justification: v3 retains original classification experiments and adds psychologist evaluations, clinically informed prompting, feature ablations, and questionnaire-score subgroup analyses.

M1.justification: Appendix D introduces a clinically informed five-shot variant that includes psychologist-selected depression markers alongside demonstration labels. The underlying classifiers, model architectures, LoRA procedure, and original explanation-generating prompts are retained.

E1.justification: The five Russian datasets, diagnostic tasks, pooled datasets, and transfer scenario remain unchanged. v3 extends evaluation coverage to clinical correctness of generated explanations on correctly classified depressed DE cases, a limited additional evaluation task using existing data.

E2.justification: Matching the full benchmark tables confirms the same AutoML approaches, four encoder models, and seven LLMs in corresponding evaluations. Changes in the best-model summary rows reflect revised rankings; the clinically informed prompt adapts an existing model.

E3.justification: v3 introduces averaging over alternative system prompts for zero-shot and five-shot evaluations, replacing the previously documented single-template evaluation. It also adds a two-psychologist, five-point explanation-rating protocol restricted to correctly detected depressed cases and BDI-score subgroup evaluations. The original 80/20 stratified split and fine-tuning hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained pooling and transfer analyses, v3 adds prompt-sensitivity evaluation, clinician-rated explanation error analysis, and a clinically informed prompt comparison. Appendix E adds Captum word ablations for label and explanation generation, while Appendix F examines performance within BDI-score subgroups.

E5.justification: Prompted LLM results change from appendix point estimates and zero-variance summary entries to means and standard deviations across prompt variants. Appendix D additionally reports Fleiss' kappa of 0.39 for psychologist agreement. The existing six-seed AutoML procedure is unchanged; the new prompt variation is not an increase in random-seed runs.

E6.justification: Many prompted results are replaced under the averaging protocol: DSM five-shot Vikhr 7B IT 0.4 macro-F1 changes from 66.06 to 63.69 ± 1.18 in Table 2. Appendix LLM precision/recall entries are also corrected. New results include explanation ratings of 2.84/5 and 2.47/5 for ordinary and clinically informed prompting, respectively, plus feature-ablation and subgroup findings.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theory, mathematical assumptions, or proofs. The added error taxonomy, agreement statistic, and feature-ablation descriptions do not introduce substantive mathematical definitions or derivations.

C1.justification: v3 adds RQ3 and a main contribution concerning clinician assessment and categorization of LLM explanations. Its conclusion now states that the evaluated explanations fail clinicians' requirements. The original model-comparison and cross-domain transfer claims remain.

C2.justification: v3 adds the substantive qualification that correct depression classifications can have clinically inadequate explanations. It interprets clinically informed prompting as potentially improving classification without resolving explanation failures, while requiring expert annotation. It also adds interpretations of influential words and BDI-subgroup differences.

D1.justification: v3 supplies a code-repository link, additional prompt templates, information about AutoML-selected Random Forest ensembles, and hardware and compute disclosures totaling 533 GPU hours in Table 9. It also provides paraphrased, anonymized DE examples. These substantially expand documentation without establishing changes to the retained training hyperparameters or raw-data access restrictions.

R1.justification: v3 adds the Captum reference for feature ablation and replaces the BDI reference with Beck et al. (1961). Most other reference changes update existing works' publication details. The positioning as a comparison of three model generations for Russian mental-disorder detection was already present in v1.

P1.justification: v3 changes the title and author information, streamlines related-work passages, and clarifies dataset and methodological prose. The existing narrative and section sequence largely remain, with Section 5.4 and Appendices D–G added for the new material.

P2.justification: v3 adds two multi-panel feature-importance figures and tables for prompt variants, compute resources, explanation errors, clinically informed prompting, subgroup results, and textual examples. Existing tables are reformatted with bold headers and captions, smaller uncertainty entries, and revised placement; Table 1 is also redesigned.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens reliability by correcting swapped precision/recall reporting and evaluating sensitivity to prompt wording. The clinician study exposes explanation failures that v1 did not assess, materially improving interpretation of potential clinical use; added implementation and resource disclosures improve transparency. The expert evidence remains restricted to one model and correctly classified depressed cases, with fair agreement. Some broad statements about prompting outperforming fine-tuning also need qualification against the updated AC results, but these limitations do not outweigh the gains.
